## Proof

**Claim:** Yes — the statement remains true. Every continuous function on $[a,b]$ can be uniformly approximated to any accuracy by a polynomial with rational coefficients.

**Setup.** Let $f \in C([a,b])$ and let $\varepsilon > 0$. We must produce a polynomial $q$ with rational coefficients such that $\|f - q\|_\infty < \varepsilon$.

**Step 1 — Approximate by a real polynomial.** By the classical Weierstrass approximation theorem (the special case of Stone–Weierstrass for the algebra of real polynomials on $[a,b]$, which separates points and contains the constants), there exists a polynomial
$$p(x) = c_0 + c_1 x + \cdots + c_n x^n, \qquad c_i \in \mathbb{R},$$
such that
$$\|f - p\|_\infty < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}.$$

**Step 2 — Approximate the real polynomial by a rational-coefficient polynomial.** Since $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, for each coefficient $c_i$ we may pick $q_i \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $|c_i - q_i| < \delta$, where $\delta > 0$ will be chosen below. Set
$$q(x) = q_0 + q_1 x + \cdots + q_n x^n.$$

For any $x \in [a,b]$,
$$|p(x) - q(x)| \le \sum_{i=0}^{n} |c_i - q_i|\,|x|^i < \delta \sum_{i=0}^{n} |x|^i.$$

Let $M := \max(|a|,|b|)$, so $|x| \le M$ on $[a,b]$, and define $S := \sum_{i=0}^{n} M^i$ (a finite, non-negative constant; if $M=0$ then $S=1$). Choosing
$$\delta := \frac{\varepsilon}{2S}$$
gives, uniformly on $[a,b]$,
$$\|p - q\|_\infty < \delta \cdot S = \frac{\varepsilon}{2}.$$

**Step 3 — Combine via the triangle inequality.**
$$\|f - q\|_\infty \le \|f - p\|_\infty + \|p - q\|_\infty < \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon.$$

**Conclusion.** For every $f \in C([a,b])$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$, we have constructed a polynomial $q$ with rational coefficients satisfying $\|f - q\|_\infty < \varepsilon$. The key mechanism is two-layer density: $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$ (coefficient level), and real polynomials are dense in $C([a,b])$ (function level, by Weierstrass). Composing these two approximations yields the desired rational-coefficient polynomial approximation. Hence the Stone–Weierstrass statement remains valid after replacing "a polynomial function" with "a polynomial function with rational coefficients."

### PROOF COMPLETE
